excerpt: The evidence layer for property decisions: a configurable scraper that collects listings into one normalized schema, keeps every run as a timestamped snapshot, and serves both bulk exports and a two-call query API — single listing, and scored comparable set with the local market's velocity attached. Market velocity from snapshot history: days-on-market, absorption rate, price-cut rate, new-supply rate

Query API — listing(url) and comparables(subject, rules): the entire contract DealScope (VC-011) runs on
Rule-based comparable matching: radius, typology, area band, condition, recency — with sample size always reported

Export to CSV, JSON, SQLite or Postgres for spreadsheets, notebooks and BI tools
Optional proxy pool: rotation, sticky sessions, geo-targeting and per-node failover
Resumable, idempotent crawls with local page caching
Polite by default: robots.txt, rate limits and concurrency caps applied per target
Scheduled runs with an alert the moment a profile stops extracting

title: FileInspector
excerpt: A cross-platform command-line utility (with an optional GUI) that lists files in a directory tree along with their metadata, exporting to JSON, XML, or CSV.
features: Cross-platform CLI — identical behavior on macOS, Windows, and Linux
Multi-format output — JSON, XML, and CSV from the same scan
Rich metadata capture — beyond name/size/dates: EXIF (photos), ID3 (audio), document properties (author, page count), and other format-specific fields
Filtering — by file name/extension, timestamp range, directory depth, file size, and file attributes
Optional GUI — builds and runs the same command the CLI accepts, for point-and-click scans
Scriptable — designed to slot into cron jobs, CI pipelines, and existing automation without a UI
Diff/compare mode — compare two scans of the same directory to see what changed
advantages: Cross-platform, where the tool it's loosely based on (FileList) is Windows-only
One tool, three output formats — no separate exporters needed per downstream system
CLI-first design means it automates cleanly; the GUI is additive, not required
Single scanning engine behind both CLI and GUI keeps results identical and halves the maintenance burden
Rich metadata capture turns a plain file listing into a genuinely useful catalog (media libraries, document archives)

Very large directory trees (millions of files) need a streaming/incremental writer, not an in-memory scan, to avoid memory blowup
Cross-platform file-attribute differences (Windows attributes vs POSIX permissions) need a normalized schema so output isn't OS-specific
XML output is rarely anyone's first choice today — worth confirming real demand before investing equal effort in all three formats
GUI must stay strictly a thin wrapper around the CLI, or the two will drift and results will stop matching

title: DealScope
excerpt: Give it a property or a development site and it answers which strategy makes the most money and how badly that changes if the assumptions are wrong — five strategies on one shared engine, ranges instead of point estimates, and a report that prints every assumption. Buyers get a fair-value band and negotiation headroom; developers get residual land value. Evidence comes from PropInsight (VC-005); DealScope never fetches a page.
features: Five strategies side by side: short-term rental, long-term rental, buy-renovate-resell, off-plan assignment, and develop-and-sell-units
One shared engine — acquisition costs, transfer tax, mortgage amortization, tax profile and horizon applied identically to every strategy
Residual land value solver: back-solves the maximum site price that still clears a target margin
Sell-out schedule driven by the local absorption rate, with finance costs tied to how long units take to sell
Unit mix and price ladder for developments, derived from local comparables
Full metric set per strategy: net yield, cash-on-cash, IRR, NPV, payback, equity multiple and break-even point
Pessimistic / base / optimistic ranges with a sensitivity tornado ranking the assumptions that actually matter
Optional Monte Carlo pass reporting the probability of clearing a target return
Assumptions derived from PropInsight comparables, each displayed with its sample size and editable in place
Confidence gating — declines to issue a verdict when the comparable set is too thin to support one
Runs standalone: full manual entry with editable per-location defaults when no comparable data exists
Buyer output: fair-value band, percentile rank against comparables, and the price at which the deal stops working
Developer output: maximum site price, sell-out schedule, and the absorption rate at which the margin disappears
Conditional verdict in plain language — worth it, under which strategy, and until what threshold
PDF report with charts, cash-flow waterfalls and amortization tables, every assumption printed on the report itself
Personalizable, forwardable reports: sender name and logo, cover note, section selection — omitted sections named as omitted
Per-jurisdiction tax and licensing rules kept in configuration files, never hardcoded
Stored analyses with durable links, re-runnable against fresh comparables to show how a deal has moved
Free with no paywalled tier or gated sections — a donation button on the finished report, unlocking nothing
The same verdict regardless of who ran it — no agent mode, no buyer mode

advantages: Answers the comparison question directly — most calculators model a single strategy in isolation
One engine across all five strategies, so the comparison reflects the strategies rather than their assumptions
Residual land value is the number a developer actually negotiates with, and almost no accessible tool produces it
Ties finance cost to measured absorption instead of an optimistic guess about sales pace
Assumptions evidenced by local comparables rather than invented, which is what makes the verdict credible
Covers contractual-position assignment, which almost no existing tool handles
Ranges and sensitivity make the risk visible instead of hiding it behind one confident number
Declines to conclude on thin evidence, which is what separates a tool from a number generator
A PDF with its assumptions printed is something a partner, accountant or lender can actually review
Serves both sides of the same table — a buyer negotiating and a developer underwriting — from one model
Pairs with PropInsight (VC-005) to evaluate a whole scraped market, not one property at a time
Free and account-free removes every reason not to try it, which is how a niche tool finds its first users
pitfalls: Garbage in, confident garbage out — a polished PDF lends false authority to bad assumptions, so they must stay visible throughout
Comparables are asking prices, not transaction prices: systematically optimistic, and the report must say so every time
Thin or heterogeneous comp sets in small markets cannot support a verdict, and the tool has to decline rather than guess
Comparability is a judgement call — renovation state, floor, view, elevator and noise rarely survive into structured fields
Renovation and build costs are where flip and development models break down; they need real quotes, not per-m² averages
Absorption measured from listing disappearance conflates sales with withdrawals, so the developer verdict must be stated as a range
Tax rules are jurisdiction-specific, change often, and are the easiest thing to get quietly wrong
Short-term-rental licensing regimes are tightening in many cities and can invalidate a strategy outright
Risk of being read as financial advice — needs clear framing and visible assumptions
Development modelling invites scope creep toward full project management, which is a different product
Anonymous third-party email sending is a spam vector and a fast route to a blacklisted domain if unguarded
Storing addresses, emails and personal financial assumptions brings GDPR duties — consent, retention, deletion, breach exposure
A free service with real marginal costs — comparable queries, PDF rendering, email — funded by donations that rarely cover them
Pressure to add an agent-friendly mode that flatters a listing, which would destroy the credibility both audiences depend on
